a: The deep ocean has yielded some of the strangest creatures ever discovered, many in the last decade, thanks to advanced submersibles and remotely operated vehicles. The yeti crab, discovered in 2005 near Easter Island, has hairy claws that look like a yeti's fur and lives around hydrothermal vents, farming bacteria on its claws for food. The barreleye fish, found at depths of 2,000 to 8,000 feet, has a transparent, fluid-filled head that allows it to see upward through its own skull, and its eyes can rotate within the transparent dome. The gulper eel, also known as the pelican eel, has an enormous mouth and throat that can stretch to swallow prey much larger than itself, and its tail is connected by a thin, thread-like structure. The anglerfish uses a bioluminescent lure to attract prey in the dark depths, with females having a glowing rod extending from their heads. The vampire squid, despite its name, is not a squid or a vampire — it's a unique creature that turns itself inside out as a defense mechanism and can survive in oxygen-poor waters by using a unique form of respiration. The blobfish, which lives off the coasts of Australia and New Zealand, has a gelatinous body that is less dense than water, allowing it to float effortlessly above the seafloor. The giant isopod, a deep-sea relative of the pill bug, can grow to over a foot long and has been observed eating entire whale carcasses. The Dumbo octopus, named for its ear-like fins that resemble Disney's Dumbo, is one of the deepest-living octopuses, found at depths of up to 7,000 feet. The snailfish, found at depths of 26,000 feet in the Mariana Trench, is the deepest-living fish ever observed. The yeti sponge, discovered in 2019 near the Galápagos Islands, forms dense forests that provide habitat for numerous other deep-sea species. These creatures have evolved remarkable adaptations to survive in one of the most extreme environments on Earth, where pressure exceeds 1,000 atmospheres, temperatures hover near freezing, and sunlight never penetrates.
